One thing I'd like clarified since the concept of backings has come up
...

The current rule regarding Jyhad vs. Vampire backings has a "hole" in
it. Section 4.1 of the tournament rules states:

If Jyhad and Vampire: The Eternal Struggle cards are both used, in
order to prevent a significant advantage, all cards from the Jyhad or
Vampire: The Eternal Struggle card sets must be of sufficiently mixed
card type - that is, Master cards must appear with both Jyhad and V:TES
card backs (or at least three different card types must have Jyhad
backs).

This means that if I decided to "cheat" I could choose 3 card types in
my deck and have them all Jyhad thus knowing when a critical
reaction/master/or modifier might be appearing.

Or I could just use Jyhad backs for my masters (all the minion taps for
example) and the rest of the masters from Vampire.

Since the rule only states what backs I must use I am able to thus play
with an effectively marked deck.

Now something is whacky here unless I've read it incorrectly.

I'm sorry you don't share my viewpoint, but I'm still pretty convinced
that it's correct. I'm not saying that VTES isn't a competive game, or
that it can't wind up hurting peoples' feelings. I'm saying that it's
just not very rigorous in terms of how much experience and training is
necessary to master it, as compared to those other activities.
Comparing VTES to Chess, guys like Ben Peal or Matt Morgan presumably
don't spend nearly the time and energy researching and innovating VTES
strategies as Grand Masters do in Chess. Continuing on the same
comparison, I consider myself a good VTES player and a decent Chess
player. I can sit down at a table with Ben Peal and win. I can't sit
down at a table with Kasparov and win. The difference isn't that I've
played more VTES than Chess, or that either of the aforementioned
players aren't at the top of their field. The difference is that VTES
just isn't as rigorous.

So my point is that if people are so crazy about competition that they
get upset by the possibility of cheating to the extent of applying
totally annoying and unnecessary rules, then they're probably playing
the wrong game.

Yeah, see, here is the crux of the issue--nobody likes cheating. Nobody
wants to encourage cheating. Everyone would be happier if there was no
cheating. This, however, does not justify draconian* measures to
prevent cheating that probably isn't happening in the first place. In
the case of card backs, you have two options:

A) Force everyone to use opaque card sleeves, which is a pain in the
ass, a lot of people don't like using, and kinda hoses folks who show
up not knowing they are required to use card sleeves till they get
there.

B) Just assume that people aren't going to cheat, and in the seldom
instance that you run into cheating, deal with it as indicated in the
tournament rules (i.e. hand out a game loss).

The likelyhood of someone cheating by virtue of abusing the card back
differences is very, very small. And if someone is going to cheat in
the first place, and they are prevented from cheating in this
particular manner, they are still likely to cheat in some other manner
(stacking deck, "forgetting" to pay pool for stuff, "accidentally"
starting the game with more pool than they are supposed to, whatever).
To the point that it isn't really worth punishing everyone (by making
them use opaque card sleeves) to try and stop unlikely cheating when it
isn't actually going to stop cheating if someone is set on cheating
anyway.

*Calling required opaque card sleeves "draconian" is certainly
hyperbolic.

-Peter

If you assume someone is going to cheat, you need to assume that they
are going to cheat. Which means that you need to, in addition to making
folks sleeve their decks, count their decks, shuffle their decks, count
their pool, check their crypts, shuffle their crypts, pay all their
costs for them, audit their pool every turn, and so on. Assuming that
the only way someone is going to cheat is that they are going to abuse
card backs, and trying to combat that, while leaving all other avenues

example) is pointless.

How is it any more obvious than abusing card backs? If anyone flips
through their deck at any point, it is very easy to notice that all of
their Masters are Jyhad or something. And if you think people won't
risk obvious cheating by marking their card sleeves, why do you think
they'll risk cheating at all? Cheating tends to be an all or nothing
sort of situation--either someone is willing to cheat (and will do so
by any means available) or they aren't. Like, I don't know what kind of
folks you play cards with, but folks I tend to run into are of the "I'm
unwilling to cheat" variety, as it is a fun card game with very little
on the line, and their sense of "I'm not a psychotic dick who needs to
cheat at a goofy CCG" vastly outweighs their sense "I MUST WIN!" So
they don't cheat either by virtue of obvious ways to cheat (i.e.
abusing card backs) or by less obvious ways to cheat (pool manipulation
and deck stacking). Why is there an assumption that people will cheat
in the first place?

> While one can always pretend he didn't think about which cards were Jyhad or not, and won't risk
> being banned out of the community.

them. Or they can pretend they accidentally started with 32 pool. Or
they can pretend that they accidentally only lost 4 pool to that bleed
when it should have been 5. It is *really* reasy to cheat in this game,
if you are inclined to do so. And really hard to catch someone cheating
(how do you know they stacked their deck? Is someone counting every
point of pool that moves in and out of their control? If they "forget"
to pass the edge, and "accidentally" collect the pool for posessing it,
and no one notices, how do you stop that?) So why bother assuming folks
are going to cheat, and then punishing everyone for it?
